Well, I've been farming these 7.5 mu for thirty years now, ever since I was a young bride. My old man and I, we know every patch of this land — which corner stays wet after rain, which strip dries out first. I never went to school, can't read much, but I can read the soil and the sky just fine.

This year, same as always, I'll put all 7.5 mu into wheat-maize double cropping. That's our bread and butter. The wheat needs to go in around October 10th, give or take. I'll use the seed we saved from last year's crop — it's local wheat, not that fancy hybrid stuff. Costs nothing but a bit of sorting, and it grows steady. I plant about 35–40 jin of seed per mu, broadcast it by hand same as my mother did.

For fertilizer, well, I don't have much cash after my youngest son's wedding last spring, and my daughter-in-law's medical bills. Urea is expensive this year. I'll put down one big bag of compound fertilizer (about 50 kg) per mu at planting — that's my base. Then if the wheat looks yellow at jointing time, maybe I'll scrape together enough for another half bag of urea as topdress. But only if it looks like it needs it. Phosphorus and potash? I just use the compound fertilizer and don't fuss with separating them. My neighbor Old Wang, he's been doing the same for years and his wheat does fine.

I'll irrigate three times for the wheat: once right after planting to get it sprouted before winter, once at green-up in March, and once at heading if the spring is dry. The well water costs money to pump, but three times is what my family has always done. Less than that and you risk it.

For maize, it goes in the day after wheat harvest, no time to waste. I plant local maize seed, about 3–4 jin per mu. One bag of compound fertilizer at planting, and if the rains are good I might not irrigate at all. But if July turns hot and dry like two years ago, I'll pump water once or twice. Maize is hardy — it doesn't fuss as much as wheat.

Labor? It's mostly me, my old man, and my second son when he's not at the factory in town. My daughter-in-law helps when she's not working her shift at the garment shop. We don't hire labor — can't afford it. Wheat harvest is the busy time, but we manage with family. The wheat and maize together, I'd say we put in about 25 family days per mu across the whole year.

I expect my wheat to give me about 400 kg per mu if the winter isn't too cold, and the maize about 450 kg per mu if the summer rains come. Last year was decent, and the year before was too. I'll take steady over gambling any day.
